'''''Barbarea verna''''' is a [[Biennial plant|biennial]] [[herb]] in the family [[Brassicaceae]].<ref name=KewPOWO>{{cite web|url= https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:1109261-2|title= Barbarea verna (Mill.) Asch.|author=<!--Not stated-->|date=n.d.|website=Plants of the World Online|publisher=The Trustees of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew|access-date= September 27, 2020}}</ref> Common names include '''land cress''', '''American cress''', '''bank cress''', '''black wood cress''', '''Belle Isle cress''', '''Bermuda cress''', '''poor man's cabbage''', '''early yellowrocket''',<ref>{{Cite book|url=http://www.forest.go.kr/kna/special/download/English_Names_for_Korean_Native_Plants.pdf |title=English Names for Korean Native Plants |publisher=[[Korea National Arboretum]] |year=2015 |isbn=978-89-97450-98-5 |location=Pocheon |pages=371 |access-date=26 January 2017 |via=[[Korea Forest Service]] |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170525105020/http://www.forest.go.kr/kna/special/download/English_Names_for_Korean_Native_Plants.pdf |archive-date=25 May 2017 }}</ref> '''early wintercress''', '''scurvy cress''', '''creasy greens''', and '''upland cress'''.<ref name="Garden">{{Cite web|date=2017-11-30|title=What's in Season: Creasy Greens|url=https://gardenandgun.com/articles/a-mountain-secret/|access-date=2020-08-22|website=Garden & Gun|language=en-US}}</ref> It is native to southern Europe and western Asia, and naturalized elsewhere<ref>{{citation |url=https://npgsweb.ars-grin.gov/gringlobal/taxonomydetail.aspx?id=105428 |title=USDA GRIN Taxonomy |access-date=8 May 2016}}</ref> It has been cultivated as a [[leaf vegetable]] in [[England]] since the 17th century. As it requires less water than [[watercress]], it is easier to cultivate.{{citation needed|date=October 2025}}

==Description==
Annual or [[Biennial plant|biennial]], winter green, [[herbaceous]] plant in the [[Brassicaceae]]. The seeds typically germinate in the autumn to form an over-wintering rosette. The following spring, it grows a main stem up to about 90 cm, sometimes up to 130 cm, which is pale green, grooved ([https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/sulcate sulcate]) and occasionally branched. The leaves are alternate and pinnate with clasping auricles at the base and between 4 and 11 pairs of sub-opposite lobes. The upper leaves have much narrower lobes than those found lower down. The whole plant is almost entirely glabrous.{{citation needed|date=October 2025}}

The flowers appear in early spring.  The inflorescence is a terminal raceme, or lateral raceme arising from the leaf axils, with 6 to 25 flowers on short 3-8mm pedicels. There are four yellowy green sepals, 5mm long and four bright yellow petals each 8mm long. Six stamens and one style with a [https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/capitate capitate] stigma at the tip.{{citation needed|date=October 2025}}

==Uses==
Land cress is considered a satisfactory substitute for [[watercress]]. It can be used in sandwiches, or salads, or cooked like [[spinach]], or used in soups or pestos.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Nyerges|first=Christopher|title=Foraging Washington: Finding, Identifying, and Preparing Edible Wild Foods|publisher=Falcon Guides|year=2017|isbn=978-1-4930-2534-3|location=Guilford, CT|oclc=965922681}}</ref>

Land cress can be grown easily in any garden. Like watercress, it loves water, but does not do well when partially submerged for long periods of time. This plant needs full sun or partial shade and moist or poorly drained soil.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Barbarea verna |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/73341/barbarea-verna/details |access-date=20 October 2023 |website=Royal Horticultural Society: Plants}}</ref> It is a common green in [[Appalachian cuisine]] as one of few plants that can [[overwinter]] in the mountains.<ref name="Garden" />

Other common names include dryland cress, cassabully, and American watercress. When cooked similarly to Southern [[collard greens]] the leaves may be called creasy greens. A variegated form is available.{{citation needed|date=October 2025}}
